title: Form Validation
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Form Validation in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Form Validation within Events, Forms, and User Input. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Real forms must support error states, loading, keyboard use, and server-side validation—not just a happy-path submit button.

content_blocks.title: Form Validation: Form data and validation
content_blocks.alt_text: Form data and validation diagram for lesson 43: Form Validation. Bind values with v-model or input events → Associate messages with each field → Show pending, success, and server errors
content_blocks.caption: Form flow: connect input state to validation and communicate both client-side and server-side errors accessibly.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Events and v-model connect user input to reactive state; validation and submission logic make forms usable and robust. This lesson focuses on Form Validation. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Required fields and constraints
items.text: For Required fields and constraints, bind the input to a clear state value, validate before submission, and associate field errors with their controls. A disabled or loading state should be reflected in the UI without treating the client as the authority for server validation.

items.title: Validating email, numbers, and text
items.text: For Validating email, numbers, and text, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Custom validation logic
items.text: For Custom validation logic, bind the input to a clear state value, validate before submission, and associate field errors with their controls. A disabled or loading state should be reflected in the UI without treating the client as the authority for server validation.

items.title: Showing field-specific errors
items.text: For Showing field-specific errors, bind the input to a clear state value, validate before submission, and associate field errors with their controls. A disabled or loading state should be reflected in the UI without treating the client as the authority for server validation.

items.title: Accessible error messages
items.text: For Accessible error messages, use semantic HTML first, ensure controls have accessible names, preserve visible keyboard focus, communicate errors in text, and verify that updates remain understandable without color or animation alone.

content_blocks.expected_output: Submitting with an address containing @ clears the simple demo error; other text shows a message. This is a teaching rule, not complete email validation.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run as App.vue. Add required attributes, focus management, server validation, and a loading state for a production form.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Form Validation with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Validating email, numbers, and text”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Events and v-model connect user input to reactive state; validation and submission logic make forms usable and robust. For Form Validation, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Form Validation” that applies “Required fields and constraints”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Required fields and constraints”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: Form Validation belongs to the broader area Events, Forms, and User Input.
The main concept to practice is Required fields and constraints.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
